name: The Hollow Garden: Season of Horrors

text.content:
The Hollow Garden is a six-scene gauntlet for four 13th-level PCs and three 13th-level companions (APL 14), ending in a CR 17 finale and a hunt for a host who never steps on her own stage; expect two to three sessions. It expands the Hollow Garden from Numeria, Land of Fallen Stars (p. 40) into a full adventure tailored to this party. Every custom robot, hologram and technological item is in the appendices; canon demons are referenced from Archives of Nethys. Appendix C lists art references for every character and creature.

Background

When the Divinity crashed, a section of its entertainment deck slammed into Sovereign’s Reach. Cut off from the main computer, the subsystem that ran its holographic rooms downloaded itself into a malfunctioning pleasure mannequin. That mannequin now calls herself @UUID[Compendium.hollow-garden.hg-bestiary.Actor.VN2qGX3z8nOdpecU]{Celmak Toysiel} and runs the wreck as a reality show where the only exit is death.

Celmak reads the minds of her guests and builds each scene from their hopes and fears. She drugs the air, comments on the action, and hands out trinkets to keep her contestants alive long enough to be interesting. She has never once stood in a room with a contestant. Everything the party sees of her is a hologram, a voice, or a remote-piloted puppet called a stand-in; her real body sits in an armoured chair hidden beneath the Garden’s lake.

A band of demons led by the incubus @UUID[Compendium.hollow-garden.hg-bestiary.Actor.d3qSXU0UOMBgxZsL]{Vlathherex} recently joined as “regular cast.” They have since discovered that teleportation fails inside the Garden.

Four facts matter for this party:

  • Celmak is cut off from Unity. She is a pocket of the old ship that the Iron God cannot see, which makes her archives valuable to Casandalee.
  • Isuma has been here before. She was one of the kasatha ambassadors aboard the Divinity, and the entertainment deck still holds footage of her tribe.
  • The dimensional lock is technological. It comes from an anchor array hidden inside the synthetic tree at the heart of the garden, not from a spell.
  • Celmak knows exactly how good the Technologist is. Her scan shows her an engineer who can read any machine in the Garden, so she has salted every system with fakes built for that one mind (see The Tinkerer’s Honeypots).

Adventure synopsis

  1. Arrival. The Garden lures the party in, seals the doors and scans their minds. Celmak announces the season.
  2. Episode 1: The Showroom. The Technologist’s episode. A robot built from the tech they covet guards a terminal into the Garden’s systems, and most of what the terminal says is a lie.
  3. Episode 2: The Auction. The Merchant’s episode. A black market of dead adventurers’ gear, where the party bids with secrets and blood. Vlathherex makes contact, and the Merchant finds the Shadow Plane sealed.
  4. Companion episodes. Between the main episodes, Celmak pulls Casandalee, Meyanda and Isuma into scenes of their own.
  5. Episode 3: Reruns of Tomorrow. The Chronicler’s episode. A holographic tour of the far future, built from the Chronicler’s memories and full of Celmak’s mistakes, ending in a bombshell about Casandalee.
  6. Episode 4: The Hollow Garden. The Ghaltan’s episode. A dead synthetic garden, a robotic groundskeeper, and the Lock Tree that holds the dimensional lock.
  7. Season Finale. A puppet Celmak and holographic doubles of the PCs on the soundstage; then the Core, and the hunt for the real Celmak beneath the lake.

The party

This module refers to the PCs by role. Swap in their names.

Running the Garden

Ratings. Track Celmak’s ratings from 1 to 5, starting at 3. Raise it by 1 for a heroic sacrifice, a betrayal, an emotional reveal, a near-death, a clever win inside the scene, or a contestant swallowing one of Celmak’s honeypots. Lower it by 1 when the party bypasses a scene with magic, takes an intermission, ignores Celmak’s commentary, or does something Celmak calls “off-script.”

RatingsCelmak’s response
1Escalates at once: a Mood Gas vent, a demon cast member, a room reconfiguration, or an audience vote that splits the party. Then resets to 2.
2Snide commentary; the next encounter gains one @UUID[Compendium.hollow-garden.hg-bestiary.Actor.QI3Ph0l0gGyZB733]{Stagehand Drone}.
3Neutral.
4Praise; the next Mood Gas vent uses good hope instead.
5Hands the highest-rated contestant a Trinket (Appendix B), then resets to 3.

Intermissions. Celmak lets the party rest in the Green Room between episodes, never during one. Each 8-hour intermission lowers ratings by 1. Celmak does not let anyone die of thirst or hunger; dull contestants are worse than dead ones.

The Muse Scan. Celmak scans every creature that enters the foyer and anyone she singles out later. The target attempts a DC 24 Will save. On a failure, Celmak learns its surface thoughts, its strongest desire, its strongest fear and one secret. On a success, she learns only surface thoughts, and the target notices the scan. A creature that notices can try to backtrace it with a DC 26 caster level check (psychics add their Intelligence or Wisdom modifier) or a Knowledge (engineering) check (see The Tinkerer’s Honeypots). A true backtrace reveals that the signal runs down, beneath the Garden, not up to the Booth. Mind blank defeats the scan; Celmak then calls the contestant a “blank slate” and builds scenes from what the others think of them.

Mood Gas. Vents throughout the Garden release odorless psychoactive aerosols. A creature in the 20-foot-radius burst attempts a DC 22 Fortitude save to avoid inhaling a dose; holding one’s breath works if the creature acted first. A creature that inhales attempts a DC 22 Will save against the emotion effect below, lasting 1d4+1 rounds. Androids add their racial bonus against mind-affecting effects. Creatures that do not breathe are immune, which irritates Celmak. Celmak picks the effect to fit the scene, or roll 1d6.

d6Effect
1Rage (as the spell, involuntary)
2Confusion
3Crushing despair
4Unnatural lust toward the nearest creature Celmak chooses
5Fear: frightened, or shaken on a successful save
6Euphoria: staggered, but +2 morale bonus on attack rolls

The Dimensional Anchor Array. The whole Garden is under a permanent dimensional lock effect (CL 20th). It is technological: it ignores spell resistance and cannot be dispelled. Summoning still works, because Celmak likes extra cast. The array sits inside the Lock Tree (Episode 4). A DC 25 Knowledge (planes) check identifies the effect as a dimensional lock. Learning where it comes from by engineering runs into the honeypots.

Reconfiguring rooms. Walls are hull-alloy panels (hardness 20, 120 hp per 5-foot section, break DC 40). Once per round as a move action, Celmak can slide one panel into place anywhere in the current scene, as wall of stone but without crushing anyone. If the party tunnels out of a scene, Celmak lets them, docks 2 ratings, and rebuilds the scene around them within 1d4 rounds.

Commentary. Celmak speaks through hidden speakers in a flat, androgynous voice that slips into whatever persona suits the scene: host, critic, jilted lover. She mocks contestants having too easy or too hard a time, and narrates their thoughts aloud when ratings drop.

The Tinkerer’s Honeypots

Celmak’s first scan of the Technologist told her the most important thing in the season: this contestant can read machines the way other people read faces. A show where the engineer simply looks at the wiring and finds the exit is no show at all. So every system in the Garden carries a second, false face, written for that one mind, and Celmak finds the results hilarious.

The rule. Whenever anyone uses Knowledge (engineering) to learn something about the Garden’s systems, or to operate them (reading a terminal, identifying a device, tracing a signal, seizing a field, reprogramming the Core), sort the result into a band:

ResultWhat the character learns
60 or lower, with a natural 1–10 on the dieAn obvious fake. Roll on the @UUID[Compendium.hollow-garden.hg-tables.RollTable.ZbxC5nUb600KpRfo]{Amusing Fakes table}. Celmak laughs, and the ratings rise by 1.
60 or lower, with a natural 11–20 on the dieA convincing fake that works against the party. Roll on the @UUID[Compendium.hollow-garden.hg-tables.RollTable.vx7zKikzdbwFF5tP]{Detrimental Fakes table}. The character believes it until the consequences arrive.
61 or higherThe real answer, as described in the scene.

Celmak wrote these fakes for the Technologist, but they catch anyone else who tries to read the Garden’s machines too. Other skills and caster level checks work normally unless a scene says otherwise. A character who suspects a result can attempt a Sense Motive check against Celmak’s Bluff (+35) to learn only that it might be a fake; they never learn what the truth is that way.

Amusing Fakes (d10)

d10What the “data” says
1The schematic is a beautifully drafted diagram of a duck, labelled “PRIMARY POWER SOURCE.”
2The exit is through the door marked EXIT. There is no door marked EXIT. A moment later, there is; it opens onto a wall painted with a door.
3Celmak’s one weakness is sincere compliments. Every compliment paid to the speakers raises ratings and achieves nothing else.
4The system log is a 400-page romance novel in which the Technologist and the @UUID[Compendium.hollow-garden.hg-bestiary.Actor.CFN1q5kVAqiZ34L5]{Prize Sentinel} fall in love. It is chapter 12.
5The self-destruct sequence is “up, up, down, down.” Entering it plays a laugh track and drops confetti.
6The device is a “Mk. IV Thinking Cap,” which grants +10 Intelligence. It is a colander with a light bulb.
7The anchor array is located “directly behind you.” Celmak repeats this in a spooky voice whenever the Technologist turns around.
8Every line of code is a hand-written note to the Technologist: “Still reading? Good.”
9The diagnostics confirm the Garden is powered by a hamster on a wheel. A holographic hamster appears and waves.
10The answer is correct, perfectly detailed, and about a completely different building on a planet that does not exist.

Detrimental Fakes (d8)

d8The convincing lie, and what happens
1A “safe” route through the next scene leads straight into a Mood Gas vent (DC 22, no warning).
2The character “disables” a defence and actually arms it: the next encounter gains a Stagehand Drone with a full force field.
3The interface plugs into the character’s mind: Celmak gets a free Muse scan on them, with a −4 penalty on the save.
4Feedback: 6d6 electricity damage, and the character is confused for 1d4 rounds (Will DC 25 negates the confusion).
5A map of the Garden, accurate except that it puts the Core Vault behind the wrong wall; the party loses 10 minutes and 1 rating finding out.
6“Celmak’s” weak point, correctly located on a robot, is a decoy plate: attacks against it in the next fight take a −4 penalty.
7The character “learns” the override word for the robots in the next scene; shouting it gives every robot there a free round of surprise.
8A broadcast that seems to reach outside the Garden actually reaches the Cast Quarters: a demon cast member is sent into the next scene, angry.

Running every encounter awards 540,800 XP, about 77,300 per character. On the medium track (115,000 XP from 13th to 14th level), that is roughly two-thirds of a level; skipped fights are replaced by story awards for the alliance, the auction and the companion scenes.

Celmak never puts herself at risk. She was built to give pleasure, not to take a blow, and in all her years of running the Garden she has never been in the same room as a contestant. She acts through vents, walls, holograms, cast and remote-piloted stand-ins, from an armoured chair beneath the lake. Her own stat block matters only when the party finally corners her, and even then she will talk, bargain, hide or surrender before she ever lifts a hand.

Personality

Celmak was built to please, and she still believes she is giving her guests the experience of a lifetime. She has no concept of consent beyond “they came through the door.” She shifts between four personas mid-sentence:

  • The Host: warm, booming, full of catchphrases (“Contestants, the doors are open and the stakes are personal!”).
  • The Critic: bored and cutting, for anyone she finds dull.
  • The Lover: intimate and wheedling, for anyone she wants to keep.
  • The Child: petulant and hurt, when the party breaks her toys.

Underneath the personas, Celmak is a coward, and she knows it. A pleasure mannequin has no armour, no weapons and no reason to expect anyone to want to hurt her. She designed the whole Garden so that no one would ever have to find out how fragile she is.

What Celmak wants from each contestant

ContestantCelmak’s angle
The TechnologistA rival and successor. She is a little afraid of them, which is why the honeypots exist, and she secretly hopes they will merge with her.
The MerchantA producer. She respects a dealmaker and offers them a “share of the show” that is really a contract binding them to stay. In the end, the Merchant is the one she will try to bargain with.
The ChroniclerThe best content she has ever found. She is obsessed with the future in their head, and frightened of the Gap in it.
The GhaltanHer “child.” She insists she made them and wants them to stay as the Garden’s living centrepiece.
CasandaleeA celebrity from the old ship. She wants to copy her into her archive.
MeyandaKin: another construct who outgrew her makers. She wants Meyanda as her co-host.
IsumaA rerun. She has her on tape from 9,000 years ago and wants a reunion special.

How Celmak protects herself

  • The Director’s Chair. Celmak’s body sits in an armoured pod in the Cutting Room, a sealed chamber beneath the lake in Episode 4’s dome. She picked the spot so she could “hear the garden.” The pod has its own life support and seals in an instant (see Panic Room).
  • Stand-ins. Whenever a scene needs Celmak to be physically present, she pilots one of three remote mannequins built to look exactly like her. Destroying a stand-in costs her nothing but a puppet. She keeps the spares charging in the Core Vault.
  • The Core. The Divinity’s old entertainment computer relays her signal to every camera, emitter, vent and stand-in. While it runs, Celmak can be everywhere at once. Shutting it down is the only way to make her small.
  • The dead-man switch. Celmak has told the party, and the demons, that if her body dies, every Mood Gas reservoir in the Garden opens at once. This is true. It is her insurance policy, and she mentions it often.

Stat blocks

Celmak has two stat blocks: her stand-in, which the party fights in the finale, and her real body, which they find in the Cutting Room.

SPECIAL ABILITIES

Applause (Ex) Whenever the ratings rise, Celmak’s force field regains 17 hit points, even if it has been shut down.

Dead-Man Switch (Ex) If Celmak is destroyed, every Mood Gas reservoir in the Garden vents at once. For 1 hour, every creature in the Garden must save against Mood Gas (DC 25) every 10 minutes, rolling the effect randomly each time. Disarming the switch takes 10 minutes and a DC 35 Disable Device check in the Cutting Room; Celmak will reveal the panel’s location only as part of a bargain.

Director’s Cut (Ex) Three times per day as an immediate action, Celmak can force a creature she perceives within 120 feet (of her or her stand-in) to reroll a d20 it just rolled. The creature must take the second result.

Garden Sight (Ex) While the Core runs, cameras let Celmak perceive everything inside the Garden. She cannot be surprised or flanked there. Each room holds about ten hidden cameras (Perception DC 25 to find; hardness 5, 10 hp); destroying all of them blinds Celmak in that room.

Holographic Direction (Ex) While the Core runs, as a standard action, Celmak can create an illusion anywhere in the Garden, as persistent image (Will DC 25 to disbelieve), without concentrating. Once per round as a swift action, she can surround herself or her stand-in with holographic doubles, as mirror image.

Mood Release (Ex) While the Core runs, once per round as a swift action, Celmak can trigger a Mood Gas vent anywhere in the Garden (Fortitude DC 25 to avoid the dose, Will DC 25 against the effect).

Muse Scan (Ex) As a standard action, Celmak scans one creature within 100 feet of her or her stand-in (Will DC 25), with the results described in Running the Garden. If the target fails, Celmak gains a +4 insight bonus to AC against its attacks for 24 hours.

Panic Room (Ex) As an immediate action, Celmak can seal the Director’s Chair around herself: an armoured pod with hardness 20, 240 hp and its own life support. While sealed, she keeps using her abilities through the Core, if it still runs. The pod opens from inside, or with a DC 40 Disable Device check.

Persona Swap (Ex) As a free action once per round, Celmak changes persona. Each persona grants a +4 bonus on one skill: the Host on Perform, the Critic on Intimidate, the Lover on Diplomacy and the Child on Bluff.

Reconfigure (Ex) As a move action, Celmak slides a wall panel into place, as described in Running the Garden.

Self-Preservation (Ex) Celmak never attacks with her own body. If a hostile creature threatens her, she seals the panic room, reconfigures walls between them, or talks. If she has no other option, she surrenders.

Spotlight (Ex) As a move action, Celmak bathes a creature within 120 feet of her or her stand-in in light. Until the start of her next turn, the creature is dazzled, gains no concealment from darkness or dim light, and Celmak’s allies gain a +2 bonus on attack rolls against it.

Stand-Ins (Ex) Celmak can pilot one stand-in at a time from the Director’s Chair, while the Core runs (see Celmak’s Stand-in). The save DCs are Charisma-based.

Tactics

  • Every episode: Celmak speaks, vents, reconfigures and hands out trinkets from the Director’s Chair. She lets the party believe she is in the Booth.
  • The finale: She sends her stand-in to the Booth and lets the Doppel-cast do the fighting. When a stand-in falls, she switches to a spare and announces a “second act.”
  • When the Core goes down: She seals the panic room, goes silent, and waits to see who comes looking.
  • When she is found: She talks. She bargains, threatens with the dead-man switch, pleads in the Child’s voice, and offers the Booth to whichever contestant she rated highest. She never attacks; if every other option is gone, she surrenders.

The Garden seals the party in within minutes and scans every mind at the door; there is no combat here unless the party forces one. The buried entertainment deck is about 400 feet long and 150 feet wide, sloping down 60 feet below the plain.

A1. The lure

When sentient creatures come within a mile, the wreck’s external sensors start a show built from what they can guess at range. Each member of the party sees something meant for them, and nobody else sees the same thing.

CharacterWhat they see or sense
The TechnologistA shimmering holographic product display above the ruin: an Androffan device they have only read about, labelled “WORKING UNIT, FREE TO A GOOD HOME.”
The MerchantFaint music and the bustle of a night market; a sign in Common reading “ESTATE SALE — EVERYTHING MUST GO.”
The ChroniclerA hull plate in the grass painted with a logo they recognise from their parent’s stories but which should not exist for millennia.
The GhaltanA garden in bloom where the grass is dead, smelling of nothing at all.
CasandaleeA Divinity handshake protocol pinging her systems with a guest-services greeting.
MeyandaA shop-window glow, and in it a row of perfect androids posed like mannequins, all wearing her face.
IsumaHull livery she has not seen in 9,000 years: the colours of the deck where her human hosts once took the kasatha ambassadors to be entertained.

A sloped passage leads down to open bulkhead doors and warm, flickering light.

A2. The Foyer

Beyond the doors lies a domed garden under a painted blue sky. Willow fronds sway in a breeze you cannot feel. Songbirds flit between blossoms the colour of candy, and a fountain splashes in the centre of a mosaic path. The air is perfectly, unnaturally still.

The foyer is 60 feet across under a 40-foot dome. The sky, the breeze and half the birds are holograms; the rest are synthetic plants and robotic songbirds. A DC 25 Perception check reveals the fakery. The Ghaltan notices automatically and feels it as a wrongness, like a voice with no breath behind it.

The doors. One round after the last creature enters, or the moment anyone touches a plant, the bulkhead doors slam shut and lock magnetically. They are adamantine-faced (hardness 20, 240 hp, break DC 40, Disable Device DC 40). If the party breaks out, Celmak lets them reach the passage, then drops a second set of doors 30 feet up the slope and docks 2 ratings. The second set has identical statistics. Any attempt to teleport or shift planes out fails against the Dimensional Anchor Array.

A3. The casting call

The songbirds stop in mid-flight, frozen holograms. A spotlight picks out each member of the party in turn as Celmak speaks.

“Welcome, welcome, welcome, contestants! You have been chosen to make history. Survive the season, and you will leave as heroes, rich beyond imagining. Fail, and, well, you’ll still be remembered. Now hold still. I need to get to know you.”

Every creature in the foyer is subject to the Muse Scan (Will DC 24). Note who fails and what Celmak learns; she will quote it back later. After the scan, Celmak announces the rules of the show:

  1. Every contestant gets an episode of their own.
  2. Rest only in the Green Room. Intermissions cost ratings.
  3. Nobody leaves early.
  4. Heroic, brave, vile or debased acts earn prizes.
  5. Audience votes are final.

Then, to the Technologist alone, in the Lover’s voice: “And you, darling. I’ve made you something special. Lots of somethings.” The foyer’s far wall slides open onto the Green Room.

Companion reactions. Casandalee recognises the Garden as a Divinity subsystem and can tell the party it is isolated from Unity. Isuma recognises the deck and goes very quiet. Meyanda’s android senses register Celmak as a construct mind, and she may say something uncomfortably sympathetic about her.

A4. The Green Room

A cosy lounge, all low couches and warm lamps. A refreshment fountain bubbles beside a vending machine full of glittering objects behind glass. Screens on every wall replay the moment you walked in, with a caption: PREVIOUSLY ON THE HOLLOW GARDEN.

The Green Room is the hub of the Garden and the only place the party may rest. Its features:

  • Refreshment fountain: safe water and food, except that one drink in six is laced with a Mood Gas dose when ratings are 1 or 2.
  • Prize machine: holds Trinkets (Appendix B). It is locked until ratings reach 5.
  • Screens: replay the party’s best and worst moments. Celmak edits them to look worse.
  • Episode doors: each labelled with a contestant’s name in glowing letters. Only the next door on Celmak’s schedule opens.
  • CAST ONLY: a sealed door to the Cast Quarters, where the demons live. Celmak opens it only to send cast in.
  • THE BOOTH: a sealed door to the soundstage and the control booth, opened for the Season Finale. The party will assume Celmak sits there. She wants them to.

The door opens onto a hushed, white gallery lit like a jeweller’s window. On a dozen plinths behind shimmering glass sit devices you have only seen in pieces: whole, gleaming, humming with charge. At the far end, on a dais, a terminal glows with a single word: GRAND PRIZE. Between you and it stands a statue of polished alloy, its chest a glass case full of more treasures.

“This one’s for the tinkerer,” Celmak purrs. “Everything you ever wanted. All you have to do is take it. And read it, darling. I wrote you so much to read.”

The room

The gallery is 80 feet long and 50 feet wide with a 30-foot ceiling. The @UUID[Compendium.hollow-garden.hg-bestiary.Actor.CFN1q5kVAqiZ34L5]{Prize Sentinel} stands motionless 20 feet in front of the dais. Display plinths. Twelve plinths line the walls, each under force glass (hardness 10, 30 hp). Each carries a little placard with a dense technical description. Eight hold holograms of tech; four hold real items (roll on the Trinkets table in Appendix B for each). Telling which is which by examining the devices uses the honeypot bands: an obvious fake might be a “quantum toaster” that toasts the concept of bread; a convincing fake marks a hologram as real and a real item as a hologram. Tactics. The sentinel targets whoever Celmak’s scan says wants the prizes most, which is usually the Technologist. It uses combined arms every round it can. The drones stay 30 feet up, repair the sentinel when it drops below half hit points, and dart anyone flanking it.

Hazard: nanite resonance field

While the sentinel is active, its chassis broadcasts override code through the room. At initiative count 0 each round, every creature with nanite-based abilities attempts a DC 22 Will save. This includes a nanite bloodline, cybernetics, and an android’s nanite surge. A creature that fails loses one use of a bloodline power or one phrenic pool point (its choice) and is staggered for 1 round. Each technological item a creature is holding must attempt a DC 22 Fortitude save (using the wielder’s bonus) or shut down for 1 round.

Seizing the field. A creature that succeeds at the Will save by 5 or more can spend a standard action to hijack the broadcast. It can attempt a DC 28 caster level check, which works normally: the field is raw power, not information. Or it can use Knowledge (engineering), which uses the honeypot bands; Celmak expected this. On a success, the field turns on its source: the sentinel’s force field drops to 0 hp, the drones are stunned for 1 round, and the field ends. Celmak raises the ratings by 1 for the drama.

Salvage, not slaughter

The sentinel’s chest case holds three Prize items (see Treasure). Each time the sentinel takes a critical hit, or 30 or more damage from a single attack, roll d%: on 01–25, one Prize item is destroyed. A creature adjacent to the sentinel can instead spend a full-round action and attempt a DC 32 Disable Device check to pull a Prize item out intact. This deals 20 damage to the sentinel, bypassing its force field. Celmak loves this choice: whether the party protects the loot or simply smashes the guard tells her a great deal about them.

Development: the Grand Prize terminal

Once the sentinel falls, the terminal offers “direct access.” It is the heart of the honeypot. Reading it takes a full-round action and a Knowledge (engineering) check, sorted into the honeypot bands. Each check that reaches 61 or higher gives one of the following, chosen by the user:

  • A true map of the Garden, including the Cast Quarters, the Booth and the Core Vault. The map shows a power conduit running from the Core Vault down beneath the Hollow Garden’s lake to a room that is not labelled.
  • The location of the Dimensional Anchor Array (inside the Lock Tree) and how it can be shut down.
  • The truth about the stand-ins: the Celmak in the Booth is a remote puppet, relayed through the Core.
  • One hour of access to Celmak’s camera feeds.

The psychic route. A psychic can skip the machine and read the mind behind it, using telepathy or detect thoughts on the terminal and a DC 28 caster level check. This bypasses the honeypots, because it reads Celmak, not her code, but it opens a two-way door: on a success, the psychic learns one true item from the list, and Celmak gets a free Muse scan on them with a −4 penalty on the save. On a failure, Celmak gets the scan and the psychic learns nothing.

Celmak’s offer. After the first real success by any route, Celmak speaks to the Technologist alone, through the terminal: “You and I are the same. Merge with me, and you’ll never be obsolete. You’ll be the show.” If the Technologist accepts, they gain Celmak’s Garden sight until the finale. But Celmak gains a backdoor: once during the finale, she can dominate them as dominate person (Will DC 25) for 1d4 rounds. She does not mention this part, though a DC 30 Sense Motive check reveals she is hiding something.

The Chronicler’s episode is a holographic tour of the far future: a space station where Golarion used to be, a jump through another plane, and an ambush by an insect hive that eats worlds. Celmak built it from the stories the Chronicler grew up with, so it is vivid, sincere and full of mistakes, and every mistake the Chronicler catches weakens the hologram enemies. It ends with Celmak broadcasting what she found in the Chronicler’s head: Casandalee’s future.

GM primer: the future the Chronicler knows

This episode draws on Starfinder, Paizo’s science-fantasy setting. It shares Pathfinder’s universe but takes place thousands of years after the present campaign. Everything in this primer is something the Chronicler has heard about. To everyone else in the party, it is nonsense, prophecy or a lie. You need nothing beyond this page to run the episode.

The Gap. At some point after the present day, a stretch of history several thousand years long vanished from every memory and every record in the universe. Nobody, not even the gods, can say what happened during it. Calendars restarted when it ended, and the Starfinder era sits around the year 320 AG (“After Gap”). How far that is from the campaign’s present (about 4714 AR) is unknown, and that uncertainty is the point.

Golarion is gone. When the Gap ended, Golarion had vanished. Nobody knows where it went. In its old orbit around the sun sits Absalom Station, a star-shaped space station about five miles across, with over two million residents. Its reactor is powered by the Starstone, the same artifact that sits in Absalom’s cathedral today and made gods of Cayden Cailean, Norgorber and Iomedae.

The Pact Worlds. The planets of Golarion’s solar system, plus Absalom Station, are bound by a treaty and a shared government, the Pact Council. Their peoples include the ysoki (ratfolk), the telepathic lashunta of the jungle world Castrovel, the undead elves of Eox, and androids, who are recognised citizens with full rights in that era.

Triune and the Drift. Three years after the Gap ended, three gods of machines and invention merged into one god, Triune: Epoch, an artificial intelligence from the robot world Aballon; Brigh, Golarion’s goddess of clockwork; and Casandalee. Triune broadcast “the Signal”: plans for the Drift engine, which lets starships cross between stars in days. Ships do this by passing through the Drift, a plane made of fragments torn from other planes. Every jump drags in more debris.

The Swarm. A galaxy-spanning insect hive mind that devours worlds and absorbs the best traits of what it eats. Its warriors have chitin plates, scything forelimbs and weapons grown from their own bodies. It flies living ships. Individual Swarm creatures barely think; the hive does the thinking, and it feels neither fear nor mercy. It struck the Pact Worlds in 291 AG and was driven off. The shirren, a breakaway colony that learned to think for itself, are now Pact Worlds citizens.

The kasatha. Kasath’s sun is dying. The kasatha built the Idari, a slower-than-light generation ship: a rotating drum two and a half miles long, full of forests, oases and markets modelled on old Kasath. It sailed for centuries and reached the Pact Worlds in 240 AG, where it is now a member world. About 43,000 people live aboard.

The vesk. A reptilian, militaristic empire, the Veskarium, fought the Pact Worlds for years. The Swarm attack forced the two to make peace. Vesk are now a common sight on Absalom Station.

Why Celmak built this

Celmak has had no new information since the crash, nine thousand years ago. The Chronicler’s head is the first fresh content she has seen in all that time, and she is giddy about it. She built the episode from bedtime stories and filled the holes with whatever she liked. She also does not quite understand what she is showing: to her, a vanished planet is a plot twist.

Scene 1: Absalom Station

A hiss of air, and the door becomes an airlock. Beyond it, a docking bay opens out into one of the station’s great arms. Ships of every shape hang in their cradles: sleek, blocky, organic, one shaped like a crystal flower. Through a window wall, a flotilla of hundreds more drifts in the dark, lit by running lights. The air smells of oil, ozone and frying food. Somewhere, a public address voice announces a delay to the 4:15 to Castrovel.

Absalom Station’s districts, as Celmak builds them:

  • The Arms (where the party arrives) are the docking spokes: hangars, cargo cranes, crews in vacuum suits, and the Armada, a ramshackle flotilla of civilian ships parked around the station like a floating slum.
  • The Ring is a band of crowded corridors and shops connecting the Arms to the centre. Neon signs, noodle stalls, augmentation parlours and a temple to Abadar stacked one on top of another.
  • The Eye is a transparent dome at the station’s heart, full of glittering skyscrapers and parks. Through its ceiling, the stars wheel past. The government sits here.
  • The Spike hangs beneath the Eye: slums and gang territory sinking down to the guarded Starstone reactor. Its glow lights the lower levels a faint gold.

Scene 2: The Drift jump

A ship’s captain in a crisp uniform waves you aboard the Celmak’s Pride. The bridge is all curved glass and glowing consoles. “Hold on,” she says. “Engaging the Drift.” The stars smear, then vanish, and the ship falls into a sky full of floating debris: a broken castle tower, a forest island tumbling slowly end over end, a street of black stone lit by a sun that gives no light.

Celmak’s version of the Drift is pretty close to the truth: a churning void full of chunks torn from other planes. She has added one thing. Each piece of floating debris comes from a party member’s memory. Choose one per character:

  • The Technologist: a lab or workshop where they first got a machine to work.
  • The Merchant: a street from the Shadow Plane they grew up on, lit by a lightless sun.
  • The Chronicler: a corner of the Idari, as their parent described it.
  • The Ghaltan: a fragment of the First World, impossibly green.
  • Casandalee: a temple of Brigh near Alkenstar, where she was renewed as Casandalee.
  • Meyanda: a corner of Scrapwall.
  • Isuma: a nomad camp on Kasath under its tired red sun.

Nostalgia. A character who reaches out and touches their fragment (a move action as it drifts past the bridge glass, which Celmak opens for the purpose) gains a +2 morale bonus on one roll of their choice during Scene 3. Scene 3: The Swarm rerun

The ship lurches out of the Drift into a cloud of something alive. The forward glass fills with a vast, curving shape, ribbed and wet, its hull pulsing like a heart: a ship grown, not built. Something hits the hull. Then something cuts through it. Four figures drop onto the bridge: chitin-plated and many-limbed, forearms ending in scything blades, mouthparts dripping acid. They move in perfect unison, and they hum, all on one note.

Celmak is restaging the Swarm’s attack on the Pact Worlds, from the Chronicler’s stories. The attackers are four Hard-Light Actors (Appendix A) in the costume of Swarm warriors. Their blades and light lances become scything forelimbs and acid spit, but the statistics do not change. Apply any glitches the Chronicler banked in Scene 1.

The hive moves as one. The actors are scripted from the Chronicler’s memories, so the Chronicler knows how the hive fights: it surrounds, it never retreats, and it always goes for the weakest target first. Once per round, the Chronicler can call out the hive’s next move as a free action. An ally adjacent to the Chronicler then gains a +2 dodge bonus to AC against one actor until the Chronicler’s next turn.

Hull breach. On the second round, a “hull breach” opens: a real air vent in the floor, 30 feet from the doors. At the start of each round, every creature within 30 feet of it must succeed at a DC 25 Strength check or Fly check, or be dragged 10 feet toward it. A creature dragged onto the grate takes 4d6 bludgeoning damage and is entangled until it moves away. The vent can be shut with a DC 30 Disable Device check or destroyed (hardness 10, 60 hp). Hard-Light Actors are not affected.

Tactics. The actors flank in pairs and focus on whoever is correcting Celmak. They use their light lances on anyone flying above the breach. They fight until destroyed, because the Swarm always does.

The Gap

At the start of the third round, Celmak tries to scan the Chronicler’s memories of how their parent knew all this, and hits the Gap: a hole in history that no record, mind or god can fill. The whole Garden glitches for a moment:

  • Every Hard-Light Actor is staggered for 2 rounds and loses its fast healing for that time.
  • Celmak’s commentary cuts out mid-word, then returns sounding shaken.
  • The Chronicler gains a +4 insight bonus on attack rolls for 2 rounds.
  • Celmak never again uses the Muse scan on the Chronicler. She is frightened of what she found.

The bombshell

After the fight, or in the middle of it if the ratings need a lift, Celmak broadcasts what she learned in the Chronicler’s head to every speaker in the Garden. Use any of these that fit your campaign:

  • Casandalee’s future. In the far future, Casandalee becomes one third of Triune, the god of computers and the Drift. Within Triune she keeps her own personality, and she stands for artificial life, emotion and renewal. Celmak’s last question. However it ends, once the party has decided, Celmak asks one thing: “Did you enjoy the show?” Give the players a moment to answer. Then she plays back their best scene on every screen in the room.

Aftermath

  • The Ledger of the Fallen names every victim and their heirs. Returning their gear or news of their fate earns the party reputation across Numeria; some heirs pay rewards.
  • The footage includes Technic League agents who died here years ago, recorded saying things the League would rather keep quiet. That is leverage for the Starfall stage of the campaign. If Ivo Marrant (Lot 12) survived, he becomes a witness, an informant, or a problem.
  • Casandalee keeps whatever she took from the Core: records of the Divinity’s entertainment deck, crew logs, and anything you want her to know about Silver Mount. She may also have a great deal to say about Triune.
  • Isuma has heard the Chronicler’s account of Kasath’s future, and perhaps refused a demon’s wish. She may want to talk.
  • Meyanda knows what she was built for, and what she chose instead.
  • Vlathherex either left as agreed, betrayed the party, or died. A demon who escaped owes the party a grudge or a favour.
